entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sayyid Sadr ad-Din Muhammad Dashtaki (died 1498 CE), often known as Sayyed Sanad, was a towering Iranian Shia philosopher and theologian whose intellectual contributions in the late 15th century firmly established him as the founder of the illustrious Shiraz school of philosophy. Flourishing in an era marked by a resurgence of intellectual activity in Persia following the Mongol invasions, Dashtaki synthesized diverse philosophical traditions, notably the Peripatetic (Mashsha'i) school of Avicenna and the Illuminationist (Ishraqi) school of Suhrawardi, into a coherent new framework. His work not only revived but also profoundly reinterpreted earlier Islamic philosophical thought, making Shiraz a vibrant center for intellectual discourse.

Dashtaki's major achievements include his extensive commentaries on canonical texts, such as Nasir al-Din Tusi's commentary on Ibn Sina's Isharat wa al-Tanbihat (Remarks and Admonitions), and his own original treatises on metaphysics, logic, and theology. He meticulously addressed complex issues concerning existence, quiddity, and the nature of knowledge, often engaging in robust debates with contemporary scholars, most famously Jalal ad-Din Davani. His method involved a critical examination of established doctrines, seeking to resolve apparent contradictions and forge a more unified philosophical system that integrated rational inquiry with mystical insight, a hallmark of the Shiraz school.
